Pregnancy

Constipation During Pregnancy: Safe Relief That Works

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Constipation during pregnancy is common and usually comes from three things: progesterone slowing your digestion, iron in prenatal vitamins firming stool, and the growing uterus crowding the bowel. For most people, relief starts with about 25 to 30 grams of fiber a day, 8 to 12 cups of fluids, and regular movement such as walking. The plan below uses real numbers, covers the iron question, and names the step-up remedies worth asking your provider about.

Why constipation shows up in pregnancy

Constipation in pregnancy is a plumbing problem, not a personal failing. Progesterone, the hormone that helps maintain the pregnancy, also relaxes smooth muscle throughout your body, including the muscle in the wall of your intestines. Food moves more slowly, the colon pulls more water out of stool along the way, and what finally arrives is harder and drier. This can start in the first trimester, long before there is a visible bump, which surprises many people. It often becomes more noticeable later, when the growing uterus starts to crowd the bowel and leaves it less room to do its job.

Prenatal vitamins add a second layer. Many formulations contain iron, which matters for building your expanding blood supply but is also well known for firming stool. Moving less, drinking less because of nausea, and eating smaller or blander meals can all reduce the fiber and fluid your gut needs to keep things going. None of this means you are doing something wrong. Constipation is one of the most common digestive complaints of pregnancy, and it tends to come and go across the trimesters. Naming the causes matters because each one points to a fix you can actually use, starting with what is on your plate.

Aim for about 25 to 30 grams of fiber a day

Most people who are pregnant do well aiming for roughly 25 to 30 grams of fiber a day, which is more than a typical diet provides. The numbers add up faster than you might expect. A medium pear with the skin has about 5 grams. A cup of raspberries has about 8. A half cup of cooked lentils or black beans has about 7 to 8. A serving of oatmeal has about 4, and a slice of whole grain bread adds 2 to 3. Prunes earn their reputation: a small handful gives you fiber plus sorbitol, a natural sugar that draws water into the bowel and helps soften stool.

Increase fiber gradually over a week or two rather than all at once, since a sudden jump can cause gas and bloating. Pair every increase with more fluids, because fiber without water can make stool bulkier but not softer. Simple swaps beat an overhaul: brown rice instead of white, a piece of fruit instead of juice, beans stirred into whatever you are already cooking. If nausea makes vegetables hard to face, fruit, smoothies with the pulp left in, and oat-based breakfasts are gentler ways in. Overall meal planning is a bigger topic than this guide, so keep the focus on fiber and let the rest of your diet be good enough.

Drink more than feels natural, and keep moving

Fluid targets in pregnancy are higher than most people expect: roughly 8 to 12 cups of water and other fluids a day, in line with ACOG guidance. Water is the workhorse, but milk, soup, and juicy fruit all count toward the total. A warm drink shortly after waking can nudge the bowel into action, because the gut is naturally more active in the morning and after meals. Warm water with lemon works, and so does a small cup of coffee, as long as you stay under the 200 milligrams of caffeine a day that ACOG considers acceptable in pregnancy. If plain water is unappealing, keep a filled bottle within reach and sip steadily instead of forcing down large glasses.

Movement matters just as much. A 20 to 30 minute walk on most days stimulates the muscles of the abdominal wall and the bowel itself, and gentle options like prenatal yoga or swimming do similar work. Two toilet habits help more than they sound like they should. First, go when the urge arrives; holding it in lets the colon pull out more water and makes the next attempt harder. Second, place a small footstool under your feet so your knees sit higher than your hips, which straightens the angle of the rectum and reduces straining. Less straining also protects you from hemorrhoids, which is a bonus worth having.

The iron question, and safe step-up options

If constipation started or clearly worsened when you began a prenatal vitamin, the iron in it is a reasonable suspect, but do not quit the vitamin on your own. Ask your provider or pharmacist about taking it with food, taking it at a different time of day, or switching to a formulation with a gentler form of iron or a lower dose if your blood counts allow it. Some people do better splitting the dose across the day. The goal is to keep the nutrients your pregnancy needs while trimming the side effect, and there is almost always a workable middle ground once you ask.

When food, fluids, and movement are not enough, there are step-up options that clinicians commonly consider reasonable in pregnancy. Bulk-forming fiber supplements such as psyllium are usually the first addition. Stool softeners such as docusate are another common choice, and a short course of polyethylene glycol is often used when things are truly stuck. Stimulant laxatives and mineral oil sit in a different category: talk with your provider before using either, since they can cause cramping, fluid shifts, or other problems. Run any product past your provider or pharmacist first, and treat this as a short list rather than a complete medication guide.

Hemorrhoids, red flags, and when to call

Constipation and hemorrhoids travel together in pregnancy, because straining and hard stool put pressure on the veins around the rectum at a time when those veins are already swollen. Everything that softens stool also protects against hemorrhoids: fiber, fluids, movement, and not sitting on the toilet longer than needed. If hemorrhoids appear anyway, warm sitz baths, witch hazel pads, and short toilet sessions usually keep them manageable. Mention them at a prenatal visit without embarrassment. Clinicians hear about hemorrhoids every day and can point you toward creams and treatments that are appropriate during pregnancy.

Most pregnancy constipation is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, but a few signs deserve more than patience. Call your clinician the same day for blood in your stool that is more than a streak on the paper, black or tarry stool, or several days without a bowel movement despite trying the steps above. Constipation that alternates with diarrhea, or pain that wakes you at night, is also worth reporting. Seek urgent care right away for severe or worsening abdominal pain, a hard swollen belly, or vomiting when you also cannot pass stool or gas, because together those can signal a blocked bowel. It can help to note bowel movement dates and what you tried in the BeMama app or on paper, so the pattern is easy to describe instead of reconstructed from memory.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Many pregnancy symptoms are common, but severity, timing, and the effect on eating, drinking, breathing, sleep, or daily function matter. Comfort measures should be low risk and medicines should be checked with a prenatal professional.

A symptom that is severe, sudden, persistent, or accompanied by bleeding, fever, vision changes, chest pain, one-sided swelling, fainting, or reduced fetal movement needs prompt assessment rather than self-treatment.

How BeMama can help

Record when symptoms begin, what makes them better or worse, and related temperature, food, hydration, or activity in BeMama. The pattern can aid communication but cannot determine whether a symptom is normal.

When to seek help

Seek urgent care for trouble breathing, chest pain, fainting, severe headache, vision changes, heavy bleeding, severe abdominal pain, fever, or inability to keep fluids down.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — Problems of the Digestive System
  • CDC — Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Progesterone, iron in prenatal vitamins, and the growing uterus all slow your gut.
  • Aim for about 25 to 30 grams of fiber a day, built up gradually with water.
  • Drink roughly 8 to 12 cups of fluids daily and walk on most days.
  • Ask about iron timing or a different formulation instead of quitting your prenatal vitamin.
  • Call your clinician about blood in stool or several days without a bowel movement, and seek urgent care for severe pain, a hard swollen belly, or vomiting.

Frequently asked questions

How can I relieve constipation during pregnancy fast?

The fastest safe options are usually a large glass of water, a warm drink, a fiber-rich snack such as prunes, and a 20 to 30 minute walk. Prunes and prune juice contain sorbitol, which draws water into the bowel and works more quickly than most foods. If a few days of fiber, fluids, and movement bring no relief, ask your provider or pharmacist about a bulk-forming fiber such as psyllium or a stool softener such as docusate. Avoid reaching for a stimulant laxative without a provider conversation first.

Is it safe to take a laxative while pregnant?

Some laxatives are generally considered reasonable in pregnancy, but check with your provider or pharmacist before starting one. Bulk-forming fiber such as psyllium and stool softeners such as docusate are the usual first choices, and a short course of polyethylene glycol is often acceptable. Stimulant laxatives need a provider conversation first because they can cause cramping, and mineral oil is best avoided because it can interfere with how you absorb fat-soluble vitamins.

Does iron in prenatal vitamins cause constipation?

Yes, the iron in many prenatal vitamins can firm stool and contribute to constipation. Do not stop the vitamin on your own, because that iron supports your growing blood supply. Instead, ask your provider about taking it with food, moving it to a different time of day, or switching to a gentler formulation or a lower dose if your blood counts allow it.

When should I worry about constipation in pregnancy?

Call your clinician the same day if you have blood in your stool, black or tarry stool, several days without a bowel movement despite home measures, or constipation alternating with diarrhea. Seek urgent care for severe abdominal pain, a hard swollen belly, or vomiting when you also cannot pass stool or gas, since those can signal a blocked bowel. Most pregnancy constipation is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, but these signs deserve prompt attention instead of more waiting.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
